content.title: About
content.content: Bao buns are soft, steamed buns made from a light wheat‑flour dough, often filled with meat, vegetables, or sweet paste. They originate from southern Chinese cuisine, especially Guangdong province. The dough is slightly sweet, and steaming gives the buns a fluffy, airy texture and a subtle aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bao buns originated in southern China as a portable snack for travelers.
The dough is leavened without yeast, using baking powder or soda for lift.
Traditional fillings include char siu pork, marinated chicken, tofu, or sweet red bean paste.
Steaming retains more nutrients compared to frying because no oil is used.
In recent years bao buns have become a global street‑food trend, often served with creative fillings and sauces.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Because the buns are steamed rather than fried, they contain less fat than many other pastries.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides a quick source of energy, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Protein‑rich when filled wisely
items.content: Fillings such as pork, chicken, tofu or beans boost the protein content, supporting satiety and muscle repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour and meat fillings supply B1, B2 and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft, steamed texture makes bao buns gentle on the digestive system, suitable for children and older adults.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat‑based dough contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rapidly digestible carbs may raise blood sugar levels, so portion control is important for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium in certain fillings
items.content: Marinated or soy‑sauce‑based fillings can be high in salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Improper storage of dough or fillings can allow bacterial growth; follow proper hygiene and temperature guidelines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve bao buns hot, split them open and add the desired filling. They can be eaten plain or with soy sauce, chili oil, and fresh vegetables. Vegetarian versions use tofu, mushrooms, and assorted veggies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked bao buns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Re‑steam for 2‑3 minutes before serving. Frozen buns retain quality for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge and then steam to refresh.

content.title: About
content.content: Blackberries, frozen are ripe blackberry berries harvested at peak ripeness and quickly frozen to lock in flavor, aroma, and nutrients. The berries are small, dark‑red, and have a characteristic sweet‑tart taste with a soft texture after thawing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blackberries belong to the rose family and are closely related to raspberries and currants.
Frozen berries retain up to 90 % of vitamin C and most antioxidants when frozen within 24 hours of picking.
In the United States, blackberries are among the most commonly home‑frozen berries.
Blackberries contain more dietary fiber than most other berries, supporting digestive health.
Anthocyanins give blackberries their deep dark‑red color and provide anti‑inflammatory benefits.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: High dietary fiber content promotes regular bowel movements and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 43 kcal, making it a good choice for weight management.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to blackberries.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although naturally sweet, people with diabetes should consider the glycemic impact.

items.title: Texture change after thawing
items.content: Thawed berries become soft, which may not be suitable for certain recipes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen blackberries can be added to smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, baked goods, sauces, or used as a topping for desserts. If needed, they can be quickly thawed in the microwave or left at room temperature for a few minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen blackberries in an airtight bag or container in the freezer at –18 °C. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Crisp, berry is a dry, crunchy snack with a berry flavor, made from whole grains and natural berry extracts. It offers a light sweetness, bright berry taste, and a crisp texture, making it a convenient snack anytime.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The snack contains only plant‑based ingredients and no artificial colourings.
The berry flavor comes from natural berry extracts, not from synthetic aromatics.
The product is gluten‑free, suitable for people with celiac disease.
Each serving provides a modest amount of antioxidants typical of berries.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Berry extracts contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: A small portion supplies energy without excessive calories.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Whole grains provide fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for individuals avoiding gluten.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Grains contain vitamins B1, B2 and B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to grain components.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although marketed as low‑calorie, the product contains a small amount of added sugar.

items.title: Not for children under 3
items.content: The crunchy texture may pose a choking hazard for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy straight from the pack, add to yogurt or muesli, or use as a crunchy topping for salads. For a warmer aroma, briefly heat in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. For extended shelf life, keep in the refrigerator to preserve crunch and flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad with light mayonnaise is a classic dish that first appeared in 1956. It is made from hard‑boiled eggs, light mayonnaise, mustard, herbs and seasonings. The light mayo contains less fat than traditional versions, keeping the creamy texture while being more diet‑friendly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The 1956 recipe became popular in post‑war America as people looked for lighter versions of traditional foods.
The original light mayonnaise was made with egg whites and a 1:1 ratio of vegetable oil, reducing calories.
The salad is often used as a sandwich filling, a side for vegetables, or part of a cold buffet.
In the 1970s many variations appeared, adding avocado, yogurt or sour cream.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin and folate, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using light mayonnaise reduces the overall calorie and fat content compared with regular mayo.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The salad supplies iron, phosphorus and selenium, important for blood health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and a modest amount of fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Mayonnaise shelf life
items.content: Light mayonnaise can spoil quickly if not stored properly, leading to foodborne illness.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared salad can be salty; those watching sodium intake should adjust added salt accordingly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg salad chilled. It can be spread on bread, used as a sandwich filling, tossed with leafy greens, or presented as an appetizer on party platters.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Over time the flavor and texture may change, so it is best made in portions.

rice-dessert-or-salad-with-fruit.title: Rice dessert or salad with fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Rice dessert or salad with fruit is a dish where cooked rice is combined with fresh or dried fruits, often accompanied by nuts, honey or yogurt. It is enjoyed in many cuisines as a light dessert, refreshing snack, or a gentle salad.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice is used in sweet dishes across Asia, the Mediterranean, and Latin America.
The rice‑fruit combination provides quick energy and natural sweetness without large amounts of added sugar.
Traditional Japanese mochi often uses glutinous rice with fruit fillings.
In some countries the rice salad is served cold during summer to refresh the body.
Fruits can be fresh or canned, allowing the recipe to adapt to seasonal availability.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice releases glucose slowly, helping maintain stable energy levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruits add vitamin C, vitamin A, potassium and dietary fiber, supporting immunity and skin health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from both rice and fruit promotes intestinal motility and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The dish typically contains little fat, making it suitable for light meals.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Phytonutrients in berries and citrus help combat free radicals.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: Some individuals may react to certain fruits such as kiwi or strawberries.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet fruits and added honey raise the glycemic index, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: Storage contamination
items.content: Improperly stored rice can develop mold or bacterial growth, especially in warm conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice dessert chilled or at room temperature, topped with fresh berries, sliced fruit, nuts, or a sprinkle of cinnamon. Dressings can include yogurt, honey, coconut milk, or a light syrup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. If the dish contains only cooked rice without fruit, it can be stored up to 5 days. Cool or reheat before serving as needed.
